teaching: A capital and a small letter can represent the same letter: A/a, M/m. A sentence starts with a capital. Names and places also start with capitals. Read each word from left to right; match the whole word rather than its first letter alone.

Put the person before the verb: “Mina works here.” Add the place or object afterwards. Use am with I, is with one person, and are with you or more than one person. Say the sentence aloud before writing it.

Listen once for the topic and the speaker’s purpose. You do not need to understand every word. Decide whether the speaker is greeting, asking for help or giving information. Then listen again for a familiar word that supports your answer.

Find who the sentence is about, then the action and the extra information. In “Mina opens the shop”, Mina is the person and opens is the action. Read again to check meaning; a familiar word alone may not tell you the whole message.

Decide what the reader needs to know. Write one idea in each short sentence. Use a simple present or future form that matches the meaning: “I live here” describes now; “I will come” describes a future plan.

Listen for the action word and the important place or object. Follow one step before moving to another. Repeat the instruction in a short phrase to check understanding. Ask “Please say that again” if you are unsure.

Say a familiar word slowly. Listen for its first sound, then blend the sounds you know. Some common words do not sound exactly as their spelling suggests. Learn a small group, cover them, recall them, and check. Use the sentence to confirm your reading.

Put a notice heading at the top and key information on separate lines. A personal message can start with the person’s name. Make the action, day and time easy to find. A clear layout helps the reader use your words.

Say who or what you are talking about, then give one clear detail. Use short sentences and leave a pause between ideas. Practise a name, a place and a simple description. Ask a partner to repeat the detail they heard.

A sign gives a short message. EXIT shows a way out; NO ENTRY means do not go in. An arrow gives a direction. A notice with a date and time often tells you about an event. Look at words and layout together, then decide what to do.

Start a sentence with a capital and finish a statement with a full stop. Write I as a capital even in the middle of a sentence. Names also need capitals. Read your work aloud and check where each complete idea ends.

Speak slowly enough to keep the words clear. In a word with more than one syllable, one part is usually stronger. Tap the beats as you say your name and a useful word. The capital part in the printed stress guide is the stronger part, not an instruction to shout.

Read digits in their written order. A room number identifies a place; a time tells you when. 10:30 means half past ten in the morning when the notice says am. A reference code identifies a record: copying one digit wrongly can select another record.

Look carefully at a familiar word, say it, cover it, write it, and check. Compare each letter in order. Keep a personal word list with fictional practice details. Practise names, common places and everyday words rather than relying only on copying.

Use a greeting and a short request: “Can you help me, please?” Ask a simple who, where or what question. Listen to the answer, then check one detail. A polite request and a clear question help the other person respond.

Decide what information you need before reading again. To find a time, look for digits and a colon. To find a person, look for a name. Point to the line that gives the answer. Check that you have copied the whole detail.

Read each field label before writing. Name asks for a person, date asks for a day, month and year, and time asks when. Use fictional details in this course. Check that each answer belongs in the field where you entered it.

Say “I like…” or “I do not like…” to express a preference. “I feel worried” describes a feeling. Let the other person finish, respond to what they said and ask a short follow-up question. Different preferences are possible.

Read the heading for the topic. Read each short sentence. Identify the purpose, one useful word and the action to take. If a word is unfamiliar, use nearby words and ask for help. Check your answer against the notice rather than guessing from memory.

Plan the reader, reason and key detail. Write a few complete sentences, choose a clear layout and check familiar spelling, capitals and full stops. Use a new detail rather than copying the worked example unchanged.

Practise asking, answering and taking turns about a familiar choice. Give a simple preference and listen to the other person’s preference. Agree on one next step. Use the partner prompts if you are alone; rehearse your replies aloud before writing brief notes.

An email often addresses a named reader; a poster gives information to many readers. Look at the heading, greeting, layout and final instruction. Ask whether the writer is informing, inviting, requesting or warning. Explain your decision using a visible feature.

Choose a message, description or notice to suit the purpose. A short email usually has a greeting, a reason and a clear ending. Use polite requests when writing to an unfamiliar person. Include the information the reader needs to respond.

Listen for the topic first, then notice words expressing feelings and preferences. “I am worried” gives a feeling; “I think…” often introduces an opinion. Do not assume a person is happy simply because they agree to a plan. Check what they actually say.

First, then, after that and finally show order. Find the start and finish before retelling what happened. A past account tells events that already happened; instructions tell someone what to do. Do not change their order when you summarise them.
Use and to add, but to contrast, and because to give a reason. Each side of a compound sentence must make sense. Avoid joining every idea into one long sentence; sometimes a full stop is clearer.

Listen for first, then and finally. Identify the order of the steps and repeat it in your own words. If a step is unclear, ask which action comes before or after it. A correct list of details in the wrong order can still lead to a mistake.

focus: Read a map and a table
teaching: Read the map key or table headings first. North is at the top of this practice map. A place directly north is one square above, not diagonally above. In a table, follow the correct row and column together before choosing an answer.

Adjectives add useful detail: a quiet room, a small red bag. In English they usually come before the noun, or after be: the room is quiet. Choose a precise adjective and explain what makes it useful to this reader.

focus: Describe and give a short account
teaching: Give the topic, relevant details and a short account in a clear order. Use because for a simple reason. A description needs useful adjectives; an account needs a sequence. Check that your sentences communicate enough information for the listener.

Related words can share a spelling pattern: book/books, help/helpful. A final s often marks more than one noun, but words such as bus already end in s. Split a longer word into useful parts, then check its meaning in the sentence.

Read the labels and any example. Use the requested format for dates and times. Check a reference code letter by letter. Answer required fields and use fictional contact details. A form is complete only when each answer matches its label.

Stress important content words rather than every word equally. A question’s intonation can help signal its purpose, but words and context matter too. Practise a short request, then ask a partner which words were easiest to hear.

A glossary explains words used in a text. Look at the first letter, then the second letter when needed: card comes before class. Find the headword, read its short definition, and substitute that meaning into the original sentence to check it fits.

Use a question mark for a direct question. Use commas to separate items in a short list. Check capitals for names, days and I. Punctuation should help the reader find sentence boundaries and understand your request.

Use who for a person, where for a place, when for time and how for a method. Make a request with “Could you…?” when you want an action. Listen carefully: a useful follow-up question responds to the answer rather than repeating the original question.

Scan for a particular name, date or word. Read the complete sentence around it to avoid mixing up old and new information. A caption explains an image. Compare the caption with the picture or map instead of treating either as the whole message.

Group words by a useful pattern, such as day/days or help/helpful. Notice that some spellings need to be remembered. Use look-say-cover-write-check, then test the word inside a new sentence. Check each letter, not just the shape.

Listen for the main point of each turn. Add a relevant statement, question or opinion. Use “I agree because…” or “I prefer…because…” to connect your contribution with another person’s idea. Take turns and check a point before disagreeing with it.

Identify purpose, follow the sequence and locate the details needed for an action. Use a glossary when a word is unfamiliar. Say which line supports your answer. If the text gives two choices, compare the stated difference before deciding.

Choose an appropriate format, explain the situation in order and include a reason. Use simple and compound sentences and a useful description. Review content first, then spelling and punctuation. Say one improvement you made.

Summarise the options, express your view, ask for the other person’s view and agree the next action. Include a reason and confirm an important detail. Review whether you responded to the actual conversation rather than delivering a memorised speech.

A narrative relates events. Notice past-tense verbs and time markers such as yesterday, later and afterwards. Find the main event and the cause of a problem. Retell in time order without adding events that are not in the account.

Plan the reader and purpose before drafting. Group related ideas into short paragraphs: situation, detail, request. A new paragraph marks a change of focus. After drafting, check that each paragraph contributes to the purpose.

Listen for the situation and purpose before collecting details. Identify the main point in your own words, then select information relevant to your question. A repeated or strongly emphasised detail may be important, but check it against the whole message.

Register is the level of formality used for a situation. A friendly message may use contractions; a formal request usually gives more explicit detail. Compare greeting, vocabulary and layout. Different forms can carry similar facts but serve different readers and purposes.

Use time markers to organise events and connectives to explain cause or contrast. A complex sentence has a main clause and a subordinate clause: “I stayed home because I was ill.” Check that the reader can follow both the order and the reason.

Identify steps, locations and conditions in an explanation. Repeat the route or process in order and check any unclear reference. Ask for clarification at the point where meaning breaks down rather than waiting until the end.

A main point is central to the message; a supporting detail explains it. An opinion expresses a judgement or preference. Distinguish what the writer thinks from what the text reports as an event. Support an answer with an appropriate quotation or accurate paraphrase.

Read instructions such as “complete this section only if…” before entering details. Decide which branch applies, then complete the relevant fields. A correct response needs consistent dates and explanations as well as complete sentences where requested.

focus: Give an account of the past
teaching: Introduce the event, explain what happened in order and describe the result. Use past forms for completed events and a reason where relevant. The listener should be able to follow the account without knowing the situation in advance.

Read all steps before acting. Notice sequence words, conditions and warnings. “Before you submit” identifies something to do earlier, not later. Check what changes when a condition applies, and explain the next step in your own words.

Choose past forms for completed events, present forms for current facts and future forms for plans. Keep the subject and verb in agreement. In a longer sentence, check each clause separately. Do not change tense unless the time meaning changes.

Use clear word stress and sentence stress to make the key detail audible. Pause between groups of meaning rather than after every word. Ask a listener to identify the detail you intended to emphasise, then adjust your delivery if needed.

A familiar subject can use specialist words such as reference, route or receipt. Look for a definition, example or contrast nearby. Test your proposed meaning in the sentence; the same word can mean something different in another context.

A complete sentence needs a main clause. Check that a subordinate clause has not been left alone as a fragment. Use capitals, full stops and question marks accurately; use commas where they help separate items or an introductory phrase.

Adapt a request to the relationship and setting. “Could you explain…?” suits an unfamiliar adviser; a friend may use a shorter question. Ask for information or advice, respond to the answer and confirm your understanding using your own words.

A dictionary entry can show a headword, word class and several meanings. Choose the meaning that fits the sentence, not automatically the first one. Check alphabetical order when locating a word. Use the chosen meaning in a new sentence.

Build a short subject word list with definitions and example sentences. Notice stems and endings and check irregular forms separately. Proofread backwards word by word for spelling after checking the meaning of the whole text.

Identify another person’s feeling or point of view before responding. Express your own view with a reason and acknowledge a difference politely. Use a clarification question or a suggestion to keep the exchange relevant and constructive.

Check purpose and register, follow events or instructions, identify the central point and locate supporting information. Use a reference entry for an unfamiliar term. Explain both your answer and how the source supports it.

Write for a new purpose using a plan, short paragraphs and a clear sequence. Include an explanation and an appropriate request or ending. Edit separately for task fulfilment, tense, sentence boundaries, punctuation and relevant vocabulary.

Rehearse the same goal first with a friend and then with an unfamiliar member of staff. Adapt greeting, register and detail. Give an explanation, ask for advice and respond to a follow-up question. Check that the next step is clear to both speakers.

A detail is stated; an inference combines clues to reach a supported conclusion. Separate a reasonable inference from a guess. For example, a request for a later slot may suggest a timing difficulty, but does not prove what caused it. State the clues and qualify uncertain conclusions.

Select relevant information, the detail needed and a suitable tone before drafting. Explain the purpose early, group supporting details logically and end with a clear next step. A formal audience needs precise, courteous language, not unnecessary difficult words.

Listen for the purpose, main points and information relevant to your task. Distinguish an example from an instruction and a suggestion from a decision. Summarise the important points without carrying over irrelevant detail.

Different genres organise information differently: a report uses headings; a narrative follows events; a leaflet may separate options. Find the structure before reading closely. Use headings and paragraph openings to locate the information relevant to your question.

Use headings for a report, a greeting and closing for a letter, and a clear sequence for an account. Link paragraphs so the reader understands the relationship between ideas. Adapt the structure to the purpose rather than using the same email shape for every task.

Identify reasons, conditions and sequence in a spoken explanation. Ask which part applies to your situation and confirm the next step. Explain the instruction to someone else so a partner can check that you understood more than isolated words.

Pronouns link to earlier nouns; connectives show cause, contrast or result. Although signals a contrast, while therefore signals a consequence. Identify what a linking word connects, then explain how changing it would change the meaning.

Read eligibility notes, conditional sections and declarations before answering. Follow the correct branch and give concise explanatory detail where requested. Check that an answer in one section does not contradict another. Use fictional details and review all required fields.

Introduce the subject, organise the main points logically and add relevant detail. Use an example or comparison to support an explanation. End with a concise summary so listeners can identify the point and the requested action.

A writer may explain, persuade, advise or complain. Notice the intended reader, requests and evaluative language. Distinguish the writer’s purpose from the topic. Identify a feature that makes the language suitable for that audience.

Use subordinate clauses to express cause, condition and contrast. A non-defining relative clause adds extra information and normally takes commas: “The office, which opens at nine, is nearby.” Keep the main meaning clear and avoid excessive clause stacking.

Change your choice of words, amount of detail and delivery to suit the audience. Practise giving the same information to a friend and to a formal group. Use clear stress and pauses, and check understanding instead of assuming the listener has followed.

Skim headings and openings for the overall point. Scan for a specific term or figure. Then read the relevant passage closely, including qualifications and exceptions. These are different strategies: scanning alone is not enough to evaluate an argument.

Check the head of the subject, not the nearest noun: “The list of dates is ready.” Use a consistent tense for the time frame, including when reporting an earlier event. Explain a tense change only when the meaning moves to a different time.

Make the purpose of your question clear. Ask for a specific explanation or action and use an appropriate register. Follow up on the answer, clarify a qualification and confirm what is agreed rather than treating the first reply as the final outcome.

Use the surrounding sentence to propose a meaning, then check a suitable dictionary or subject glossary. Compare entries when a term has more than one sense. Record the sense and an example that fits this source, rather than copying an unrelated definition.

Check common irregular spellings as well as subject vocabulary. Use punctuation to make sentence boundaries and extra information clear. Proofread in separate passes so correcting spelling does not distract you from a missing verb or an unclear paragraph.

Follow the topic, connect your contribution to earlier turns and give a relevant opinion. Acknowledge an alternative view before responding. Use suitable listening signals, such as a brief acknowledgement or appropriate eye contact where comfortable and accessible.

Locate information in two formats, compare what each contributes and make a supported inference. Check vocabulary using reference material. A complete answer explains the relevant evidence and any uncertainty instead of simply repeating a phrase.

Plan and produce a text suited to a new reader and purpose. Develop relevant reasons, use paragraphs and a range of controlled sentences, and make the requested action explicit. Explain your revisions using specific examples from your own draft.

Compare options with a partner, explain your view and invite theirs. Resolve a difference by suggesting a practical compromise. Summarise who will do what and when. Check how verbal and non-verbal signals helped or hindered understanding.

focus: Main ideas and a concise summary
teaching: Identify the central claim and the function of each paragraph. Separate examples from conclusions. A summary preserves the argument and important qualifications in fewer words; it should not introduce your own opinion or copy every detail.

Decide the audience, purpose, evidence and level of detail. Order the argument before drafting and identify what each paragraph must achieve. Distinguish established information from a proposal or inference. A strong plan includes a limitation or alternative viewpoint where relevant.

Track the main argument and supporting detail across a longer contribution. Distinguish information, interpretation and recommendation. Note what the speaker leaves uncertain. Summarise the position fairly before evaluating it.

A report, advertisement and personal account can present the same issue differently. Locate specific details in each and check dates, scope and qualifications. Organisational features help you find evidence; they do not establish that a claim is reliable.

Choose a format and style that serve the reader. Use linking expressions precisely: however contrasts, therefore draws a consequence, and for example illustrates. Refer clearly to earlier ideas and vary sentence openings without losing the logical thread.

Listen for all steps, deadlines, exceptions and cross-references. Identify which branch applies to a stated situation. Repeat the sequence and condition in your own words, then ask a focused question about any ambiguity.

A claim presented as a fact may still need evidence. Opinions evaluate or recommend. Infer an unstated meaning from several clues, identify alternative explanations and avoid treating an inference as certainty. Separate the writer’s claim from the evidence offered for it.

Check conditional questions, exemptions, date ranges and supporting explanations together. Follow cross-references and complete every relevant branch. Keep your declaration consistent with the information entered. If an instruction is ambiguous, explain what needs clarification rather than inventing a fact.

focus: Present and develop a detailed case
teaching: Organise a detailed explanation or argument, use relevant evidence and choose language suitable for the audience. Include a comparison or limitation. Respond to a request for clarification by adding relevant detail, not merely repeating the original wording.

Compare who produced each source, its purpose, evidence and limitations. Two sources can disagree because they use different samples or measures. Identify agreement and disagreement, then explain which claim is better supported and what further information would help.

Choose clauses and voice to express the intended relationship. A past counterfactual uses if + past perfect and would/could have + participle. Reported speech and passive forms can change focus, but must preserve meaning and appropriate tense.

Use a range of tenses, sequence markers and conjunctions to make relationships clear. Distinguish what happened, what is happening and what might happen. Rehearse an account with a hypothetical alternative and ask a listener to explain the difference they heard.

Notice evaluative words, register and grammar that position the reader. Explain how a chosen word contributes to purpose or tone. Compare a neutral alternative with the original and test whether it changes the strength or implication of the claim.

Check tense relationships, agreement, pronoun reference and clause boundaries throughout a longer text. A complex sentence is useful only if its meaning remains precise. Read a revised sentence in its paragraph to ensure the correction has not changed the claim.

Ask for the detail needed for a decision and adapt the request to the setting. Use an embedded question politely where appropriate. Explain why you need clarification and confirm the answer without changing its qualifications.

Use section headings, numbered clauses, contents and cross-references to find the right passage. Resolve specialist vocabulary using an appropriate entry and context. Keep an exception with the rule it qualifies; missing that exception can reverse an answer.

Check specialist and irregular spellings, then punctuation in simple and complex sentences. Use commas for clause structure, a colon to introduce an explanation where appropriate, and apostrophes accurately. Explain how an edit removes ambiguity rather than merely making the text look formal.

Support an opinion using the supplied evidence and identify its limitations. Respond to a contrasting argument accurately and respectfully. Invite another contribution, ask a relevant follow-up question and help the group return to the issue if it drifts.

Summarise a longer document, compare it with a second source and distinguish supported conclusions from unresolved questions. Explain how purpose and language affect presentation. Use reference material where needed and preserve important limitations in your final synthesis.

Produce a developed text for a defined audience, using appropriate genre conventions and a clear sequence. Support a position with the supplied evidence, consider a different view and qualify conclusions where needed. Review grammar, spelling, punctuation and the effectiveness of the whole response.

focus: Move a discussion towards an outcome
teaching: Compare positions, identify common ground and propose an evidence-based next step. Include a possible disadvantage and respond to a follow-up challenge. Summarise the outcome and any unresolved question so the discussion moves forward without pretending that every difference is settled.
